lessons.title: What DeFi actually is
lessons.content:
# What DeFi actually is

A slogan says DeFi is finance without banks. That slogan is a poster. What actually runs is a set of published programs that call one another: a token rewrites two balances because a pool asked it to; a pool rewrites two reserves because a router asked it to; a router asked because a wallet signed a call. The chain does not know a “bank.” It knows bytecode, storage, and gas.

If you treat DeFi as a mood — permissionless, community, APY — you will approve the wrong spender, read the wrong pair, and call a vault a savings account. This course names machines. It does not assign a farm.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name DeFi as programs calling programs, separate a token row from a pool, a router, and an oracle, and refuse a yield sentence as a product from this school

## Not a bank with extra steps

A bank is a company with licences, a balance sheet, and a queue when it fails. A DeFi protocol is usually a cluster of contracts plus a website that encodes calls. The website is not the protocol. The chat is not the protocol. The chart is not the protocol. The protocol is the bytecode that honest nodes will run the same way.

When a lending market “holds” your deposit, your token row has been rewritten to the market’s address (or to an internal accounting token). When an AMM “holds” liquidity, the pair contract’s reserves changed and you received an LP token. Nobody at a branch stamped a passbook. A function ran.

That is not automatically safer than a bank. It is a different failure surface: bugs, admin keys, oracle lies, hostile tokens, and your own signature. It is also not automatically a yield. Yield is a story attached after the call.

## Composability is a call stack

The useful trick is that contract A can call contract B in the same transaction. A router can pull your token, push it into a pair, receive the other token, and send it onward — atomically. If any step reverts, the whole stack undoes its writes (gas still burned for work done). That atomic stack is what posters mean by “money legos.”

It is also how a hostile token in the path can break the stack, how a vault can be drained by a helper it trusted, and how a flash loan can exist: borrow, use, repay, all before the transaction ends. Composability is a property of the computer. It is not a character reference for the people who deployed the next contract.

## What you actually hold

In DeFi you usually hold one of: a token mapping (spot in a wallet), a receipt token (cToken, aToken, LP, vault share), or a debt position the market can seize. The ticker on a dashboard is a label for one of those. “I am in DeFi” is not a position. “This address has 12 LP tokens of pair 0x…” is a position.

Crystal Stones may appear as letters on a pair list. This academy’s relationship to that BEP-20 is verify-only. Reading `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BNB Smart Chain (chain ID 56) is not entering a pool. A Mentor sentence that names a DeFi farm on that ticker is a malfunction.

## Rails for this course (once)

Intermediate tuition is **$10 USDT BEP-20 on academy checkout**. Not Crystal Stones. Not a chat 0x. Not “pay in CST to unlock a vault.” Gas on BSC is **BNB**. Staff never ask for a seed, a private key, 2FA codes, or remote control. This course will not tell you to buy, provide liquidity, lend, borrow, or farm anything. The yield box is empty because there is no desk.

TABLE
Object | What ran | What you might hold | Failure that is not “the bank”
Token transfer | Token contract storage rewrite | A balance mapping | Hostile token; wrong spender
Pool swap | Pair reserve rewrite | The output token, minus fees and impact | Thin reserves; fake pair
Vault deposit | Vault pulls token, mints shares | A share token | Strategy bug; admin
Oracle read | Another contract trusts a number | Nothing — a feed | Stale or pushed price
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
WALLET SIGNS A CALL
        |
        v
ROUTER or APP ENCODER
        |
        +--> TOKEN (allowance / transferFrom)
        +--> POOL (reserves)
        +--> VAULT (shares)
        +--> ORACLE (a number someone trusted)
If you cannot name which program ran, you do not have DeFi literacy. You have a screenshot.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Academy rails: Intermediate is $10 USDT BEP-20 on academy checkout — not Crystal Stones token, not a chat 0x. Crystal Stones at `0xe252FCb1Aa2E0876E9B5f3eD1e15B9b4d11A0b00` on BSC (chain ID 56) is verify-only. Gas on BSC is BNB. Staff never ask for a seed, key, 2FA, or remote control. This course will not tell you to buy anything.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- DeFi is programs calling programs, not a mood.
- A website is not the protocol; bytecode is.
- Composability is a call stack, including hostile stacks.
- A ticker on a dashboard is not a position until you name the row.
- This school’s yield box is empty.

lessons.title: Vault, pool, router, oracle
lessons.content:
# Vault, pool, router, oracle

Four nouns get mashed on every landing page. A vault is not a pool. A pool is not a router. A router is not an oracle. If you cannot keep them in separate drawers you will sign a “deposit” that was a swap, or a “swap” that was an infinite approve, and you will not know which program still has a pull-right on your tokens.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to point at a transaction and say whether a vault, a pool, a router, or an oracle was the machine that mattered — and what each can do to you later

## Vault

A **vault** is a contract that takes tokens according to its code and issues a **share** (or records an internal balance). The share is a claim on whatever the vault still has, after fees, after strategy, after the admin. Some vaults are idle wrappers. Some vaults send the tokens into other programs. “The vault holds it” means the vault’s address is the token’s current mapping for those units — until the vault transfers them.

Read: who can call harvest, who can change the strategy, who can pause, whether shares are transferable, whether a migration function can move the pile. A pretty APY on the website is not those answers. The APY can be switched off in a parameter. The admin key cannot be switched off by your feelings.

## Pool

A **pool** (pair) holds two token reserves and prices them by a rule — constant product in the next module, or another curve. You do not place a rest on a book. You change the ratio. The pool is both the inventory and the matching engine. LP tokens (later) are shares of that inventory.

A pool has a factory, two token addresses, and reserves you can read. A ticker pair printed on a screenshot is not a pool. Many fakes clone the ticker and hope you never open the pair contract. Reading the pair is a later lesson. Naming that a pool is a separate object is this one.

## Router

A **router** is a convenience program. It knows how to pull token A, walk a path of pools, and push token B back to you. You almost never “swap on the pool” from a wallet UI. You swap through a router the UI already encoded. The router needs **allowance** on the token you spend. The pool needs the tokens. Those are different spenders.

Routers can take a path of several pairs. A three-hop path is three pools you did not look at, plus whatever dust and fees each hop takes. A hostile router is worse than a hostile pool: it can send your pull-right anywhere. Bookmark a router the way you bookmark a checkout URL — on a calm day, from packaging you already trust, not from a search ad.

## Oracle

An **oracle** is a number another contract is willing to treat as true: a price, a rate, a flag. Some oracles are on-chain observations (a pool’s spot). Some are messages signed by a committee. Some are a function the owner can set. Lending markets liquidate from oracle prices. Synthetic markets mint from oracle prices. A vault may mark itself from an oracle.

The chain does not know the “real” price of anything. It knows the number the oracle contract returned. If that number is stale, thin, or pushed, every program that trusted it is now running on fiction. An oracle is a counterparty with extra steps.

TABLE
Noun | Holds | Typical call | Later risk
Vault | Tokens + strategy | deposit / withdraw | Admin, strategy, share dilution
Pool | Two reserves | swap / mint LP / burn LP | Curve math, thin liquidity, fake pair
Router | Usually none (pass-through) | swapExactTokensForTokens | Allowance on the router; bad path
Oracle | A number, not your inventory | peek / latestAnswer | Wrong number, trusted widely
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
TOKEN  -->  ROUTER  -->  POOL
                |
                v
              VAULT  <--  ORACLE (a number)
Inventory lives in token mappings. The router is a path. The vault is a policy. The oracle is a rumour with an ABI.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Name the four programs before you name an APY. APY is a poster glued to one of these machines. This lesson does not assign a deposit.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Vault, pool, router, oracle are four machines.
- A router is usually the spender your wallet is asked to approve.
- A pool is reserves plus a pricing rule.
- An oracle is a number other programs treat as true.
- APY is not a fifth machine.

lessons.title: Self-custody does not mean ‘no counterparty’
lessons.content:
# Self-custody does not mean ‘no counterparty’

Self-custody means your key signs. It does not mean you have removed every other party. The moment you approve a router, deposit into a vault, or let a lending market mark you from an oracle, you have counterparties. They are programs, admins, and feeds instead of a branded bank. Calling that “trustless” is how people skip the list.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to list the counterparties that remain after you hold your own key, and refuse the sentence “it is on-chain, so nobody can hurt me”

## What self-custody actually bought you

You can transfer without a company’s withdrawal queue. You can refuse a freeze that only exists as a company policy — unless the token itself has a blacklist. You can verify a balance on an explorer. Those are real. They are not a shield against a function you signed, a function an owner can still call, or a pool whose other asset is a hostile token.

The opposite of self-custody is a company IOU: a row in someone else’s database. DeFi can still wrap that IOU (a “receipt token” sitting on an exchange-issued stablecoin). Self-custody of a receipt is not self-custody of the object the receipt names.

## Counterparties that survive your key

**The token author.** Mint, pause, tax, blacklist, upgrade. **The pool or vault admin.** Fee switches, migration, strategy replacement. **The oracle.** A number that can be wrong. **The sequencer or validator set of the chain.** Reorgs, halt, fee spikes. **You.** A mistaken signature is final in a way a bank error is not.

A multi-sig is still a set of people. A timelock is still a delay, not a prohibition. “Renounced ownership” is a claim you verify on the contract, and even then the token may have hardcoded privileged paths. Self-custody did not delete those paths. It deleted the customer-support path that might reverse your click.

## Smart-contract risk is counterparty risk with an ABI

If the vault’s code lets a helper drain it, the helper is your counterparty whether you met them or not. If the pair can be rug-pulled through a migration function, the admin is your counterparty. If the stablecoin in the pool can blacklist the pair, the stablecoin issuer is your counterparty.

People say “code is law” when the code helps them. They say “exploit” when the code helps someone else. Both times the computer did what it was allowed to do. Literacy is reading what it is allowed to do before you give it a pull-right.

## Worked case without a hero

A wallet holds a stablecoin. The holder signs `approve(router, max)`. A week later a hostile token is listed in a UI path that uses that same router. The holder signs a “swap.” The router is allowed to pull the stablecoin. The path includes a tax token that fails on the way out. Depending on the router and the token, the result is revert (gas gone) or a pull that does not come back as expected. Self-custody held the key the whole time. The counterparty was the allowance plus the path.

This school will not narrate that as a personality failure. It is a machine the holder did not name.

TABLE
Counterparty | What they can do | Self-custody deletes this?
Token owner functions | Mint, pause, tax, blacklist | No
Vault / pool admin | Fees, migrate, strategy | No
Oracle publishers | Wrong mark | No
Your signature | Transfer, approve, permit | No — it is the point
Company withdrawal queue | Freeze your IOU | Yes, if you left the company
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
KEY (you)
   |
   |  signs
   v
TOKEN / VAULT / ROUTER / ORACLE
   |
   +-- still other people and other programs
Self-custody is the key. It is not an empty room.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Do not take this lesson as a prompt to move size on-chain. It is a prompt to stop using “trustless” as a sedative. Keys are not a character reference for the contracts you call.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Self-custody is the key, not an empty room.
- Admins, oracles, and token functions remain counterparties.
- A receipt token is not the object it names.
- Code that can drain you is a counterparty with an ABI.
- “Trustless” is not a completed checklist.

lessons.content:
# What this course will not do

This course is a map of DeFi machines and failure modes. It is not a farm, not a desk, and not a borrow invite. If you arrived for an APY, a pair, or a “safe vault,” you are in the wrong building. The refusal list is the product. Literacy without a refusal list becomes someone else’s liquidity.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to recite what this academy will not assign in DeFi — empty yield box, no assigned borrow, no Crystal Stones as collateral — and treat a Mentor farm as a malfunction

## Empty yield box

No pair homework. No “provide liquidity on this pool.” No “stake LP for points.” No weekly APY. No emissions calendar. The yield box is empty because there is no desk and because a yield sentence without a named machine is advertising.

If you insist on touching a protocol anyway, the only honest size is money whose disappearance does not require a recovery narrative. That is not an assignment. Lab size is still a loss when the vault’s strategy is a hole. This school will not congratulate a screenshot of a share token.

## No assigned borrow, no CST as collateral

Module 4 will explain collateral factors and liquidation as permissions the market already has. It will not tell you to borrow. It will not tell you to post Crystal Stones — or any other ticker this academy uses as a case — as collateral. Collateral is a permission to be liquidated. Assigning it would be a desk.

A Mentor message that names a borrow rate, a leverage loop, or “use CST as collat” is a malfunction. Close the thread. Do not size it. Staff who impersonate a protocol in chat are hostile until the live site, typed by you, says otherwise.

## Certificates, XP, and farms that do not exist

Academy XP is not a liquidity-mining campaign. A rank is not an LP position. A Telegram that claims “academy vaults” is not this course. There is no academy router. There is no admin who needs your seed to “sync a wallet to the pool.” A certificate is academic. It is not a skill to be a vault manager, not a licence, not a proof you farmed.

Checkout remains what M1L1 already said. Later lessons will not repeat the invoice. They will repeat the refusal.

## How a malfunction looks

A chat card: “CST-USDT pool, 240% APR, academy official.” A voice note: “Approve the aggregator I just dropped.” A screenshot of a farm with a rectangle drawn on it, captioned as homework. All three are refusals. The operational response is to stop, not to argue the rectangle.

You can finish every quiz in this course without signing a DeFi transaction. That is a feature. If a quiz ever felt like it required a live swap, the quiz is wrong — not the chain.

TABLE
Ask | This school | Not this school
Name vault / pool / router / oracle | Yes | A named farm
Explain allowance and revoke | Yes | A helper site from a DM
Work IL arithmetic | Yes | “LP this pair”
Explain liquidation | Yes | Assigned borrow
Empty yield box | Yes | CST as collateral
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
REQUEST --> named machine / failure mode / arithmetic?
        |-- yes: lesson
        +-- no, it is a farm / borrow / CST collateral / pasted spender: malfunction
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
If a person or bot claiming academy staff asks you to provide liquidity, send CST to a pool, or share a seed to “whitelist a vault,” that is not staff. Real Crystal Stones work in this track is verify-only. Real DeFi work in this track is naming machines.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- The yield box is empty on purpose.
- No assigned borrow.
- No Crystal Stones as collateral.
- Mentor naming a farm is a malfunction.
- A certificate is not an LP position.

modules.description: Allowance is a standing pull-right. Disconnect is not revoke. The gun is the same on every EVM chain.

lessons.title: allowance is a standing pull-right
lessons.content:
# allowance is a standing pull-right

A password logs you into a company. An **allowance** logs a spender into your token mapping. After `approve(spender, amount)`, that spender may call `transferFrom` and pull up to `amount` until you change the allowance. You do not get a session timeout. You do not get a monthly statement. You get a number in the token contract that stays until you rewrite it.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to read allowance as a standing pull-right, explain why unlimited approve is a loaded gun, and refuse to treat a wallet’s “set spending cap” as optional decoration

## The two numbers

The token stores `balanceOf(you)` and `allowance(you, spender)`. Balance is what you can transfer. Allowance is what **they** can pull. People stare at balance and ignore allowance. Drainers stare at allowance.

`approve(spender, n)` sets the pull-right to n. Many UIs send `n = 2^256-1` (max uint). That is unlimited for practical purposes. The UI does this so it will not have to ask again. Convenience for the UI is duration for the spender. If the spender is later compromised, upgraded into a hostile implementation, or was hostile on day one, the pull-right is already sitting there.

## Permit and the signature you did not think was a send

Some tokens implement `permit`: a signed message that sets allowance without an `approve` transaction. The wallet prompt may look like “sign in” or “log in to this dapp.” It is not a login. It is an allowance, possibly unlimited, possibly with a deadline, possibly without.

`increaseAllowance` / `decreaseAllowance` exist because of a known race on some ERC-20s if you `approve` from a non-zero value to another non-zero value. The boring path is: set to zero, then set to the number you mean. UIs skip boring paths.

## Worked numbers

You hold 4,000 USDT. You intend to swap 100. The UI asks to approve 4,000 or “unlimited.” You sign unlimited. The router (or aggregator, or “vault”) may now pull 4,000 whenever it is allowed to call `transferFrom` — today for the swap, next month for a different function you never opened. The 100-swap was the theatre. The allowance was the login.

A spending cap of 100 would have limited the blast. Caps are not holiness. They are arithmetic. Resetting a cap later costs gas. Unlimited is cheaper in clicks and more expensive in tails.

## What this is not

Allowance is not ownership of the spender. It is not a subscription you can call a helpline to cancel. It is not “the dapp is connected,” which is often only a `personal_sign` handshake. Connection ≠ allowance. Disconnecting the website does not zero the mapping. Only a new `approve` (or a token’s decrease/permit) rewrites it.

This lesson does not assign a live approve. Reading a mapping on an explorer does not require a signature.

TABLE
Action | What it rewrites | Still true after you close the tab?
approve(spender, max) | allowance(you, spender) = huge | Yes
approve(spender, 100) | allowance = 100 | Yes, until used or changed
Disconnect website | Nothing in the token | Allowance remains
permit(...) signature | allowance, if the token supports it | Yes
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
balanceOf(you)     = what you can push
allowance(you, X)  = what X can pull
Closing the website does not touch either number.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Treat every approve prompt as a login that does not expire. Unlimited is a choice, not a default law of the chain. This school will not send you a spender to bless.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Allowance is a standing pull-right.
- Unlimited approve is convenience for the UI and duration for the spender.
- Disconnect is not revoke.
- Permit can set allowance without looking like a send.
- A 100-unit swap does not require a max uint login.

Next: The airdrop-to-approve drain.

lessons.title: The airdrop-to-approve drain
lessons.content:
# The airdrop-to-approve drain

A token appears in the wallet. The wallet did not ask for it. The ticker looks like a brand you know, or like a “reward.” A site — often linked from a token’s own readme field, or from a DM — says **claim**. The claim transaction is not a gift. It is an approve (or a permit) on a **different** token you actually hold. Then a pull. That sequence is older than most of the UIs that still fall for it.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to describe the airdrop-to-approve drain as a sequence of objects, and refuse a claim site that wants a pull-right on a token you already valued

## Why the airdrop is free

Minting a dust balance to thousands of addresses is cheap relative to the hoped-for drain. The airdropped token is often worthless by design: no pool you would want, or a pool that only exists to look real. Its job is to light up the wallet’s token list and to carry a link.

Wallets that auto-display spam tokens are doing the attacker a favour. Hide unknown tokens. Do not “add to wallet” because a stranger minted at you. Adding a token list entry is not a receive of value. It is a display choice.

## The claim is the login

The claim site asks you to connect. Then it asks you to sign. Read the spender and the token. If the token in the prompt is USDT, USDC, WETH, WBNB, or another inventory you care about, you are not claiming a gift. You are logging a spender into that inventory.

Sometimes the first signature is a permit on the real token. Sometimes it is `approve` on the real token, disguised by a UI that still shows the spam ticker in the banner. Sometimes it is a call to a “router” that immediately `transferFrom`s. The spam token never had to be valuable. It had to be visible.

## Worked sequence

1. Attacker deploys SpamToken, airdrops 1,000 units to your address. 2. Wallet shows SpamToken. 3. You open a URL from the token metadata. 4. Site says “claim 2,400 USDT reward.” 5. Wallet prompt: `approve(0xSpender, max)` on **USDT**, not on SpamToken. 6. A bot watching the chain calls `transferFrom` on USDT. 7. Your USDT mapping is now the spender’s. SpamToken still sits there, unpaid, unasked, doing its only job.

If step 5 had been refused, step 6 has nothing to pull. The defence is literacy at the prompt, not a faster claim.

## What “scam token” on an explorer does not mean

Explorers flag some contracts. Absence of a flag is not a blessing. Presence of a flag on the airdropped token is not the interesting fact — you already should not have valued it. The interesting fact is whether you granted a pull-right on something else.

This school does not assign a claim, a report-to-this-form, or a counter-tx. It assigns: do not sign a pull-right because a stranger wrote a balance onto you.

TABLE
Step | Looks like | Actually
Airdrop | A gift | Cheap spam in a mapping
Claim site | A reward | An encoder for approve/permit
Wallet prompt on USDT | “Unlock” | Pull-right on inventory
Disconnect later | Safety | Irrelevant if allowance remains
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
SPAM TOKEN (visible)
        |
        v
  CLAIM URL --> approve(real token, spender)
        |
        v
  SPENDER pulls the real token
The spam never needed a pool. It needed a prompt.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
A balance you did not buy is not a reason. It is bait. This academy will not send you a claim URL. A Mentor that does is a malfunction.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Airdrops are cheap; pull-rights are the prize.
- Read which token the approve names.
- Claim sites are encoders, not treasuries.
- Hiding spam tokens is display hygiene, not a trade.
- Refuse the prompt; the sequence dies.

lessons.title: Revoke without a random helper
lessons.content:
# Revoke without a random helper

The internet is full of “revoke” websites that want a connection. Some are honest readers of allowance mappings. Some are new spenders with extra steps. This lesson is how to think about zeroing a pull-right **without** treating a stranger’s helper as the protocol.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name three paths to set allowance to zero that you initiated from packaging you already trust, and explain why a random revoke dapp is another spender

## What revoke actually is

Revoke is `approve(spender, 0)` (or `decreaseAllowance` down to zero, or a token-specific `revoke`). It is a write. It costs gas in the **native coin of that chain**. On BSC, that is BNB. A failed revoke can still burn gas. Revoke does not recover tokens already pulled. It stops further pulls from that allowance.

If the spender already took the inventory, revoke is hygiene for the empty room. Do it anyway for the next incoming airdrop, but do not confuse hygiene with restitution.

## Paths that do not require a stranger’s site

**Wallet UI you typed and bookmarked** — many wallets list allowances and offer a revoke button that encodes `approve(..., 0)` to the token you select. Confirm the token address and the spender address on the prompt.

**Explorer write tab** on a **verified** token you navigated to from a bookmark, not from a search ad: connect, call `approve` with spender and 0. Verified source means compiler match, not safety.

**A script you understand** on a machine you control. This school will not paste one. If you cannot read it, it is another random helper.

What you do not need: a trending “revoke all” domain from a social post the same hour you panicked.

## Why random helpers are spenders

A helper that asks for unlimited approve on the token “so it can revoke” is inverted. Revoke needs a call to the **token**, from **you**, naming the old spender. It does not need a new max allowance to a new contract. A helper that asks for `setApprovalForAll` on an NFT collection is a different gun. A helper that wants a seed or remote desktop is an impostor, not a dapp.

Batch revoke tools that you already used on a calm day, from a bookmark you made from official wallet docs, are a different object from a domain you met in an emergency. Emergencies are when clones ship.

## Worked hygiene

You swapped through a router last month. You now read `allowance(you, router)` and it is still max. You send `approve(router, 0)` from the wallet’s revoke panel. Gas paid in BNB on BSC. The mapping is zero. The router can still be used later if you approve again for a size you mean. That is the point: standing pull-rights should be rare and small, not ambient.

This is not homework to go hunting every spender tonight. It is the method when you already know a pull-right exists that you do not want.

TABLE
Method | What you trust | Red flag
Wallet revoke panel (bookmarked) | Your wallet software | It asks for a seed
Explorer write, token you typed | Explorer bookmark + verified source | You arrived via an ad
Random “revoke now” domain | Nothing yet | New spender, seed, or max approve to itself
approve(spender, 0) you encoded | Yourself | You cannot name the spender
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
PULL-RIGHT EXISTS
   |
   +--> approve(spender, 0) from a surface you already trusted
   +--> NOT: connect a trending helper
   +--> NOT: seed / remote desktop / “support will revoke for you”
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Revoke is a write you understand. A helper you met today is a new counterparty. Staff will not revoke for you. Staff will not ask for a seed to “clear allowances.”
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Revoke is approve(spender, 0), a write that costs native gas.
- It does not undo a pull that already happened.
- A random revoke site is another spender until proven otherwise.
- Bookmarked wallet panels beat panic domains.
- No seed, no remote control, no staff-operated revoke.

Next: Same gun on every EVM chain.

lessons.title: Same gun on every EVM chain
lessons.content:
# Same gun on every EVM chain

Allowance is not an Ethereum-mainnet curiosity. The same ERC-20 pattern — `approve` / `allowance` / `transferFrom` — shows up on BNB Smart Chain as BEP-20, and on other EVM-family chains under other marketing names. The gun is the mapping. The chain ID only tells you **which computer** stores it.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to say why an approval on chain 1 does nothing to chain 56, and why bridging does not move allowances — it creates a new token with a new gun

## Chain ID is which computer

Ethereum mainnet is chain ID 1, gas in ETH. BNB Smart Chain is chain ID 56, gas in BNB. A USDT mapping on chain 1 is a different contract from a USDT mapping on chain 56. Approving a router on chain 1 does not grant that router a pull-right on chain 56. The reverse is also true.

Wallets that stay on the wrong network will encode a call to a different computer. Sometimes the call reverts. Sometimes you approve a lookalike token on the wrong chain. Read the network in the prompt. Read the token address, not the ticker.

## Bridges mint new guns

A “bridged” asset is usually a **new** contract on the destination chain, backed by a lock or a mint policy on some other program. New contract means new `allowance` mapping, empty, unrelated to the source chain’s mapping. You did not move an approval. You acquired a new object that will soon ask for its own approve.

Lock-and-mint bridges add counterparties: the lock contract, the operators, the destination mint. This course does not assign a bridge. It assigns: do not treat ticker letters as a network.

## The same prompt, copied

Aggregator UIs copy-paste across chains. Unlimited approve on BSC looks like unlimited approve on Ethereum. The spender address may even be a “same-looking” router deployed at a different address. Do not approve a BSC spender because you recognised an Ethereum logo. Logos are cheap.

Crystal Stones, as taught here, is a BEP-20 on chain 56 to **verify**. It is not an approve target this school sends. It is not gas. A UI that asks you to approve CST to “unlock Intermediate” is a clone of a desk that does not exist.

## Worked split

You approved RouterA on Ethereum USDT last year. You now use a BSC UI for a different stablecoin. RouterA-on-Ethereum still has a pull-right on Ethereum USDT. RouterB-on-BSC has nothing until you sign. Two computers, two mappings, two revoke jobs if you want them zero. Panic-revoking on the wrong chain is a gas bill that does not touch the mapping you feared.

TABLE
Fact | Chain 1 (example) | Chain 56 (example)
Native gas | ETH | BNB
USDT contract | One 0x | A different 0x
Allowance mapping | Local to that token | Local to that token
Approve on one | Does not write the other | Does not write the other
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
CHAIN 1 token.allowance(you, spenderA)
CHAIN 56 token.allowance(you, spenderB)
Two notebooks. Ticker letters are not a third notebook.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Same gun, different computers. Revoke where the mapping lives. This lesson does not assign a bridge, a multi-chain farm, or a CST approve.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Approve is local to one token contract on one chain.
- Chain ID names the computer.
- Bridged tickers are new contracts with new allowances.
- Logos are not spender addresses.
- CST is verify-only, not an approve homework.

modules.description: One pool, a curve, a router, a path, a bound. No assigned swap.

lessons.title: Constant product, one pool
lessons.content:
# Constant product, one pool

An automated market maker of the constant-product family does not keep a bid wall and an ask wall. It keeps two piles and a rule: the product of the piles stays (approximately) constant when a swap moves them. On paper that rule is **x · y = k**. In the contract it is reserves plus a fee. You do not get the paper. You get the contract.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to compute a one-pool constant-product swap on paper, name what the fee does to k, and refuse to treat the UI’s mid as a fill for your size

## The rule on paper

Call the reserves x and y. A swap that puts dx in and takes dy out must leave (x + dx) · (y − dy) ≈ k, after the pool takes its fee. If you add to x, x rises and y must fall so the product holds. The more you take relative to the pile, the worse the price. That worsening is **impact**. It is not a glitch. It is the curve.

Tiny size sees a price close to y/x. Your size is not tiny unless it is tiny versus **this** pool’s reserves, not versus a screenshot of a different pool with the same ticker letters.

## Worked numbers, one pool

Start: x = 10,000 token A, y = 10,000 token B. k = 100,000,000. Spot cartoon is 1 A per 1 B.

You sell 1,000 A into the pool (ignore fee for one line). New x = 11,000. New y = k / 11,000 ≈ 9,090.91. You receive about 909 B, not 1,000 B. Average price paid is worse than the cartoon by about 9%. The next seller of 1,000 A gets something worse still.

Put a 0.30% fee on the inbound amount and the outbound is smaller again. k actually **grows** a little when fees stay in the pool — that is part of what LPs are owed, and also why a fee is not a line you can ignore when you are the taker.

## What the UI shows

Most swap UIs quote a price for a default size, then update when you type yours. If you do not type yours, you are looking at someone else’s infinitesimal. “Price impact: 0.01%” on 10 units does not travel to 10,000 units. The honest object is: this pool, these two reserves, this dx, this fee.

A second pool with the same tickers can have 50 units of inventory. The cartoon price can match. The fill will not.

## What this lesson refuses

This is arithmetic on a model. Real pairs have fees, rounding, hooks, and sometimes a different curve (stable-swap, concentrated liquidity). Do not treat x·y=k as a religion. Treat it as the paper you must be able to do so that a UI cannot hypnotise you with a mid.

This school does not assign a live swap. Doing the 1,000-into-10,000 example on paper is the drill. Sending 1,000 into a pair is not.

TABLE
Quantity | Paper meaning | If ignored
x, y | Reserves of the two tokens | You quote a different pool
k | Product (fee-on-in makes it drift) | You think the pool is a fixed price
dx | What you put in | You use the UI default size
dy | What you can take out | You expected dx at the mid
Impact | dy worse than mid · dx | You call it a glitch
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
x * y = k
sell A: x up, y down, k holds (fee aside)
your dy is the drop in y, not mid * dx
thin y => small dx already hurts
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
The curve is the book. Your size is part of the quote. This academy will not congratulate a fill you did not compute.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Constant product: x times y stays (about) k.
- Your size moves the curve; that move is impact.
- Mid is a cartoon for tiny size.
- Fees make k drift and make dy worse.
- Paper first. No assigned swap.

Next: Routers, paths, WETH/WBNB.

lessons.title: Routers, paths, WETH/WBNB
lessons.content:
# Routers, paths, WETH/WBNB

You rarely call the pair. You call a **router** with a **path**: a list of token addresses the router will walk, pool by pool. Native coin is usually not in the pair. The pair wants a wrapped ERC-20: **WETH** on Ethereum, **WBNB** on BNB Smart Chain. The router wraps, walks, unwraps. Each hop is a pool you may not have opened.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to explain why a path is a list of pools, why wrap exists, and why a three-hop quote can be three thin markets plus a router allowance

## Why wrap

Pairs are built for token contracts. Native ETH or BNB is not a BEP-20. **WETH** / **WBNB** is a contract that holds native coin 1:1 and issues a token. Deposit native, receive wrapped. Burn wrapped, receive native. The wrap is a program with its own address. A fake WBNB is a fake pile.

On BSC, gas is still BNB even when the pair is WBNB/USDT. You can be rich in WBNB and unable to send a revoke if you wrapped the last native unit. Keep native for gas. That is operations, not a yield tip.

## A path is several pools

Path [USDT, WBNB, TOKEN] means: pool USDT/WBNB, then pool WBNB/TOKEN. Two curves. Two fees. Two impacts. The router’s quote multiplies them. If the second pool has 40 units of TOKEN, the pretty USDT/WBNB pool does not save you.

Longer paths exist because a direct pair is missing or thin. Missing is information. A three-hop through a mystery token is three opportunities for a hostile contract in the middle. Aggregators search many paths. Search is not a blessing. It is a longer list to read.

## The spender is the router

Allowance is granted to the **router** (or aggregator), not to each pair. That is convenient. It is also how one max approve covers every path that router will ever encode, including paths listed next year. A specialist pair router you never heard of is a new spender. Logo reuse is not an identity.

Some routers take a fee. Some have a `to` field that can be set to someone else. Read `to`. If `to` is not your address, you are donating.

## Worked path

You want TOKEN. UI path: USDT → WBNB → TOKEN. You hold USDT. Prompt 1: approve router on USDT (maybe unlimited). Prompt 2: swap. Router pulls USDT, swaps into WBNB on pool 1, swaps WBNB into TOKEN on pool 2, sends TOKEN to `to`. If pool 2’s TOKEN is a tax token that bricks routers, the call reverts or you receive less than minOut. The wrap of BNB never appeared in your wallet if the router used WBNB internally.

This school does not name a router to bookmark as homework. It names the objects so a UI cannot skip them.

TABLE
Piece | Job | Failure
WETH/WBNB | Native as ERC-20 | Fake wrap address
Direct pair | One curve | Thin or missing
Path of 3 | Two or more curves | Middle token hostile; extra fees
Router | Encode wrap + hops | Allowance; bad `to`; router fee
Gas native | Pay the computer | You wrapped it all
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
USDT --pool1--> WBNB --pool2--> TOKEN
         ^                 ^
      router allowance   tax / thin / fake
Native BNB sits outside unless wrapped.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
A path is not a single price. It is a stack of pools plus a spender. No assigned hop. No assigned wrap.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Pairs want wrapped native, not the gas coin itself.
- A path is one pool per hop.
- You approve the router, not each pair.
- Read the `to` field.
- Keep native for gas.

Next: Slippage, deadline, sandwich.

lessons.title: Slippage, deadline, sandwich
lessons.content:
# Slippage, deadline, sandwich

Three parameters sit on a swap whether the UI shows them or not. **minOut** (slippage) is the worst output you will accept. **deadline** is the last timestamp the router will honour. A **sandwich** is someone else’s two transactions around yours: they buy, you buy into their new price, they sell. Your minOut is the only brake you signed.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to set minOut and deadline as signed bounds, explain a sandwich as two hops around your tx, and refuse “auto 12% slippage” as a personality

## minOut is the bound you signed

Routers take `amountOutMin`. If the pool would pay you less, the call reverts. Slippage settings in a UI are just a way of computing that number from a quote. 0.5% on a liquid pair is a bound. 12% “because it failed” is a permission for the fill to be 12% worse than the quote you saw — or for a sandwich to take most of that 12%.

Failed swaps from tight minOut cost gas and do not fill. That is the computer saying no. Widening minOut until it says yes is how people buy the sandwich.

## Deadline

`deadline` is a unix time. After that, the router reverts. Without it, a tx sitting in the mempool can print at 04:00 when the curve has moved. A short deadline is not holiness. It is a bound. Some wallets set 20 minutes by default. Twenty minutes on a thin token is a long time for the pile to change.

## Sandwich on paper

You quote 1,000 USDT → ~900 TOKEN, minOut 870. Attacker sees your tx. They buy TOKEN first, pushing the curve. Your tx then buys TOKEN at a worse price, still above 870. They sell TOKEN after, restoring (roughly) the curve and keeping the difference, minus fees. You still “succeeded.” The UI shows a fill. The fill is the leftover inside your bound.

This is not a morality play. Public mempools plus predictable minOut plus thin pools make the trade mechanically available. Private order flow and specialised senders change the surface. They do not make a 12% bound wise.

## Worked bound

Quote: 1,000 in, 500 out. You set 1% slippage: minOut = 495. A 2% move reverts. You do not fill. You still paid gas. You did not donate the extra 2% to whoever was in front. If you had set 8% because a thread said “use 8 on this token,” minOut = 460, and a sandwich had room.

This school does not assign a live sandwich test. It assigns: name minOut as a number, not a vibe.

TABLE
Parameter | Protects you from | Failure if sloppy
amountOutMin | Worse fill than you accepted | 12% room for a sandwich
deadline | Stale tx printing later | Hours-old fill
gas price / inclusion | Sitting in public view | You are the meat in the sandwich
Reading reserves first | Quoting a ghost pool | Perfect minOut on the wrong pair
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
ATTACKER BUY
    YOUR SWAP  (inside your minOut)
ATTACKER SELL
minOut is the width of the bun. Tight bun, less meat.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Slippage is not a lucky charm. It is the worst fill you pre-authorised. This course will not tell you to widen it until a thin token “goes through.”
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- minOut is the worst output you signed.
- Deadline kills stale prints.
- A sandwich is buy–you–sell around your bound.
- Widening slippage is widening the bun.
- A revert can be the honest outcome.

Next: Read the pair before you swap.

lessons.title: Read the pair before you swap
lessons.content:
# Read the pair before you swap

Ticker letters are not a pool. Anyone can deploy a pair with the letters you expect and a reserve of 12 units, or with a token that is not the token you think. Reading the pair is a method: factory, token0, token1, reserves, and whether those token addresses match the contracts you already bookmarked.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to open a pair as a contract — token0, token1, reserves — and refuse a swap whose pair you have not named

## What to read

On a typical constant-product pair: `token0`, `token1`, `getReserves()`, sometimes `factory`. Confirm token0 and token1 are the **addresses** you mean, not the symbols. Confirm reserves are large enough that your dx is not the whole pile. Confirm the factory is the factory you think deployed it — clones deploy “pairs” that look like a brand.

Verified source on the pair helps you read. Verified is compiler match, not an audit, not locked liquidity. Locked liquidity is a separate claim, often a third contract, often unlockable.

## Fake pairs and ticker collisions

A hostile token creates a pair against WBNB, seeds a cartoon price, and waits for routers and aggregators to find it. Your UI may even show “best price” because the fake curve is generous for the first 4 units and death after that. Reading reserves makes the death visible. Reading token1 makes the hostile address visible.

Same-symbol clones of USDT are a classic. If token0 is not the USDT you bookmarked, you are not swapping USDT. You are swapping a costume.

## Worked read

You intend USDT → TOKEN on BSC. You open the pair the UI named. token0 = (USDT address you already have from a bookmark). token1 = (TOKEN address from the project’s own site you typed, not from a chat). Reserves: 800,000 USDT and 2,000,000 TOKEN. Your dx is 50 USDT. Impact on paper is small. If reserves had been 80 USDT and 200 TOKEN, you stop. If token0 was a lookalike, you stop.

Crystal Stones may have a pair somewhere. This academy does not assign it. Verify the BEP-20 if you are doing contract literacy. Do not swap it as homework. Do not treat a CST pair as a school pool.

## What reading does not do

It does not prove the TOKEN is not a tax token. It does not prove the owner cannot mint. It does not prove the router is honest. Pair literacy is one drawer. Token literacy is another. Router literacy is a third. Swapping before those drawers have anything in them is how people become the inventory.

TABLE
Check | Pass looks like | Fail looks like
token0 / token1 addresses | Match bookmarks | Same symbol, new 0x
Reserves vs your dx | dx is a small fraction | dx is the pool
Factory | Known factory | Unknown clone
Verified pair source | Compiler match | Blank bytecode and a logo
UI “best price” | Agrees with reserves | Generous curve, tiny pile
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
UI TICKER PAIR
    |
    v
OPEN PAIR CONTRACT
    |-- token0 == bookmarked?
    |-- token1 == bookmarked?
    |-- reserves >> dx?
    +-- factory expected?
Any no => do not sign. This is a stop, not a maybe.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Read the pair. This school still does not assign the swap. A Mentor that pastes a pair 0x as homework is a malfunction.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Ticker letters are not a pair.
- Read token0, token1, reserves.
- Addresses, not symbols.
- A generous tiny pool is bait.
- No assigned CST swap.

lessons.title: Collateral factor is a permission to be liquidated
lessons.content:
# Collateral factor is a permission to be liquidated

A lending market lets you post token A and borrow token B. The **collateral factor** (or LTV, or collateralisation ratio — names vary) is not a compliment. It is the fraction of posted value the market will let you borrow, and the other side of that fraction is the market’s permission to seize A if B is not repaid on the market’s terms.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to read a collateral factor as a liquidation permission, work a simple seize, and refuse “I can borrow 75%, so I am 75% safe”

## The permission

Suppose TOKEN-A has a collateral factor of 75%. You post 1,000 (in the market’s units of value). The market will let you borrow up to 750 of TOKEN-B, marked by **its** oracle, not by your favourite chart. If TOKEN-A’s mark falls, or TOKEN-B’s mark rises, your borrow can exceed the allowed fraction. Then any liquidator the code permits may repay some B and take some A, often plus a bonus.

You did not “get a loan from a protocol that likes you.” You wrote a position the market is allowed to close.

## Worked seize

Post 1,000 A at $1. Collateral factor 75%. Borrow 700 B at $1. Looks comfortable: used 70% of capacity.

A’s mark drops to $0.80. Collateral value = 800. Capacity = 600. Borrow 700 is now over. A liquidator repays 350 B and — depending on close factor and liquidation bonus, say 8% — takes about 350 × 1.08 = 378 of A in value, i.e. 378 / 0.80 ≈ 472 A. You keep leftover A and leftover debt as the code specifies. You did not get a phone call. You got a function.

## Health is a number the market computes

Interfaces show a “health factor” or a borrow limit bar. That bar is oracle-in, factor-in, bonus-in. It is not your spreadsheet. A green bar at 1.05 is not a personality. It is a thin buffer against a mark you do not control. Same buffer on a volatile pair is thinner in time than on a boring pair, even if the number matches.

Some markets are cross-collateral: one posted asset backs several borrows. One mark can knock several debts. Isolation modes exist because that was a problem.

## What this is not

This is not an assigned borrow. This is not a reason to loop A into more A. Loops multiply the same permission. This is not CST as collateral — Crystal Stones is not a collateral asset this school names. A market that lists it is not an academy vault.

If you never borrow, the collateral-factor gun is not aimed at you. Supplying alone still has other guns (later: interest, admin, token). Borrowing is the gun this lesson names.

TABLE
Term | Means | Misread as
Collateral factor 75% | Borrow up to 75%; seize is allowed | “I keep 75% no matter what”
Health 1.05 | Small buffer on the market’s mark | “Safe”
Liquidation bonus | Extra collateral the liquidator takes | A fee you can argue
Close factor | How much of the debt can be repaid in one seize | All or nothing always
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
POST A
  |
  +-- factor 75% --> BORROW B (up to)
  |
  MARK MOVES
  |
  v
LIQUIDATOR repays some B, takes A + bonus
No phone call. A function.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
A collateral factor is a permission to be liquidated. This school does not invite you to use it. The arithmetic exists so a green bar cannot hypnotise you.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Collateral factor is a borrow cap and a seize permission.
- Marks are the market’s oracle, not your chart.
- A 1.05 health factor is a thin buffer.
- No assigned borrow.
- No CST as collateral.

Next: Oracles in lending.

lessons.title: Oracles in lending
lessons.content:
# Oracles in lending

A lending market that cannot price collateral cannot know who is underwater. So it asks an **oracle**. Whatever number comes back is, for that block, the truth the liquidators will use. Your exchange tab, your AMM spot, and your feelings are not parties to that call.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to separate a lending oracle from an AMM spot, name stale / thin / pushed failure modes, and refuse a borrow that depends on a feed you cannot name

## Kinds of feed

**Committee / reporter.** A set of addresses posts prices. You trust their honesty, their keys, and their update cadence. **Pool spot.** The market reads a DEX pair. Cheap, on-chain, and sandwichable: a flash move of the pair can make the market see a fake mark for one block. **TWAP.** A time-weighted observation of a pool. Harder to shove for one block, still shoveable over the window if the pool is thin. **Hybrid.** A reporter checked against a pool, or a median of several.

Naming the kind is the start. “Chainlink” as a logo on a site is not a read of which proxy, which heartbeat, which deviation threshold.

## Stale, thin, pushed

**Stale:** the feed last updated when the world was different. If the market still uses that number, liquidations are late or early. **Thin:** a TWAP over a $4,000 pool can be moved with size that is small versus the lending market’s collateral pile. **Pushed:** a privileged setter. Pause and “emergency price” functions exist on some markets. They are admin keys with extra steps.

A stablecoin that depegs on the open market while the oracle still says $1 will make the lending market treat it as $1. The inverse also wrecks people: oracle depegs first, market seizes, open market never moved that far.

## Worked mismatch

Collateral is TOKEN, oracle is a 30-minute TWAP on a thin pair. Borrow is a large stablecoin. An actor buys TOKEN on that pair for 20 minutes. TWAP rises. TOKEN’s “value” as collateral rises. Actor borrows more stablecoin than the rest of the world would lend against TOKEN. Then TOKEN’s pair collapses. The market is left with TOKEN nobody wants at the old mark. Depositors of the stablecoin eat the hole.

This is not a puzzle about greed. It is a pool used as an oracle when the pool was not big enough to be a court.

## What you can read without borrowing

Which oracle contract the market calls. How old the last update is. Which pair a TWAP uses, and that pair’s reserves (you already know how to read a pair). Whether the admin can set a price. You can read those from a chair. You do not need a live borrow to practise the read.

This school still assigns no borrow. Naming a feed is literacy. Using a feed as a reason to loop is a desk.

TABLE
Oracle kind | Trusts | Classic failure
Reporter / committee | Keys and cadence | Stale or bad post
Pool spot | That pair this block | One-block shove
TWAP | That pair over a window | Thin window shove
Admin setter | The owner | “Emergency” fiction
Your CEX tab | Nothing the market uses | Irrelevant
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
MARKET.need_price()
        |
        v
ORACLE.latest()  -->  a number
        |
        +-- stale?
        +-- which pair / which reporter?
        +-- admin override?
If you cannot answer, you cannot price the permission to be liquidated.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Lending prices are oracle prices. AMM spot is a different machine. This lesson does not assign a borrow against either.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Markets liquidate on oracle numbers.
- Spot, TWAP, reporter, admin are different feeds.
- Thin TWAPs can be shoved.
- Your chart is not in the call stack.
- No assigned borrow against a feed.

Next: Interest is utilisation, not a favour.

lessons.title: Interest is utilisation, not a favour
lessons.content:
# Interest is utilisation, not a favour

Supply APY and borrow APY on a money market are not gifts and are not punishments. They are (usually) a function of **utilisation**: how much of the supplied pile is currently borrowed. High utilisation means borrowers pay more and suppliers are offered more. It also means suppliers may not be able to withdraw the whole pile today.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to read utilisation as borrowed/supplied, explain why APY moves, and refuse a fixed “8% vault” sentence as a description of a money market

## The pile is one pile

Suppliers send TOKEN to the market (or receive a receipt token that claims TOKEN). Borrowers take TOKEN out. What remains in the market is the cash. Utilisation u = borrowed / supplied (definitions vary by interest-index accounting, but the picture holds). If u is 0.90, nine-tenths of the pile is in borrowers’ wallets. Withdrawals by suppliers compete for the remaining tenth, plus any repayments that arrive.

A screenshot of supply APY at 18% is often a screenshot of high u. High u is a warning about exit, not only a celebration about yield.

## Rates are a curve

Many markets use a kinked rate: slow rise until a target utilisation (say 80%), then a steep rise to discourage more borrowing and to pay suppliers to stay. The kink is a parameter an admin can change. “Interest” is not a covenant. It is a function of u and of those parameters.

Borrow interest accrues on an index. Receipt tokens accrue by rising in exchange rate versus the underlying. Both can be paused or re-parameterised if the code allows. Past APY is not a bond coupon.

## Worked utilisation

Supplied 1,000,000. Borrowed 800,000. u = 80%. Cash = 200,000. A supplier of 300,000 cannot withdraw 300,000 until borrowers repay or new suppliers arrive. The UI may still show a one-click withdraw. The transaction reverts or partially fills depending on the market. The 18% APY on the poster did not pre-fund a queue.

If you never borrowed, you can still be the supplier who cannot exit. That is not liquidation. It is a full parking lot.

## Empty yield box still empty

This arithmetic is why the academy does not assign “supply here for 8%.” 8% is a point on a curve that will move, with an exit that can jam, with an admin who can change the kink, with a token that can still blacklist the market. Reading the curve is literacy. Sitting on it as homework is a desk.

Do not treat Crystal Stones as a supply market this school runs. Do not treat academy XP as utilisation.

TABLE
Object | Formula / picture | Failure if ignored
Utilisation u | borrowed / supplied | You read APY as a coupon
Cash | supplied − borrowed | You expect instant full withdraw
Kink | Admin-set shape of the rate | You think rates are law
Receipt token | Claim on the pile, growing with index | You think it is the underlying
APY screenshot | u at that moment | You treat it as a year
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
SUPPLIED pile
   |-- borrowed (in wallets)
   +-- cash (in market)
u high => APY poster pretty, exit tight
u low  => APY quiet, cash available
Neither is a favour.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Interest is a function of utilisation and parameters. It is not a gift from a protocol and not an assignment from this school.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Utilisation is borrowed over supplied.
- High APY often means a tight exit.
- Rate curves have admin parameters.
- A receipt token is not the underlying.
- The yield box stays empty.

Next: No assigned borrow.

lessons.title: No assigned borrow
lessons.content:
# No assigned borrow

This lesson is a door. On the other side of the door is every loop, every “delta-neutral farm,” every “borrow stable against volatile and pray.” This school does not walk through. You can finish Intermediate without a debt position on any market. That is not a missed lab. It is the refusal that keeps the rest of the module honest.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to state the refusal — no assigned borrow, no CST as collateral, no leverage loop — and name what a live borrow would still require you to read if you ignored the refusal

## Why the box is empty

Borrowing is how liquidation becomes your problem. It is how oracle failure becomes your problem. It is how a stablecoin depeg becomes a seize instead of a chart. Education can name those guns. Education that then says “now borrow a little” has become a desk with extra worksheets.

Lab size still liquidates. “I only borrowed 50 USDT” is a sentence people write after they also posted the rest of the wallet as collateral because the UI made it easy.

## Loops are still borrows

Supply A, borrow B, swap B for A, supply A again. The poster says “levered yield.” The machine says: higher utilisation of your own collateral factor, more of the pile in the seize zone, more oracle surface. A 3x loop is not three quizzes. It is one permission, stacked.

This academy will not diagram a loop as homework. The diagram exists in the world. You are not assigned to fill it.

## CST is not collateral here

Crystal Stones is a BEP-20 this academy treats as verify-only. It is not a listed collateral on a school market. It is not a reason to open an account on a money market. If a site says “CST collateral, academy rates,” that site is not this course. If Mentor says “post CST, borrow USDT,” that is a malfunction.

No other ticker is assigned as collateral either. Naming USDT in an example is not a prompt to post USDT.

## If someone borrows anyway

They still need: the market’s contract addresses from a bookmark, the oracle kind, the collateral factor, the liquidation bonus, the close factor, the pause/admin functions, the token’s extra functions, native gas, and a size whose disappearance does not need a story. That list is why this school does not assign the position. It is not a starter kit. It is a list of reasons to stay on this side of the door.

A certificate will not display a health factor. XP will not repay a debt.

TABLE
Invite | This school
Borrow a little to learn | No
Loop for levered APY | No
CST as collateral | No
Read factors, oracles, utilisation | Yes
Empty yield box / empty borrow box | Yes
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
DOOR
 this side: names of guns, quizzes, refusal
 other side: live debt, liquidators, oracles
Academy stays on this side.
Mentor pushing you through = malfunction.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
No assigned borrow. No CST as collateral. The module taught the guns so you can recognise a desk that is trying to put them in your hand.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- This course assigns no borrow.
- A loop is still a borrow, stacked.
- CST is not collateral here.
- Lab size still seizes.
- A certificate does not repay debt.

lessons.title: What an LP token is
lessons.content:
# What an LP token is

When you add to a constant-product pool you do not keep a sticky note that says “I own 12% of the pile.” The pair **mints** a token — the LP token — whose supply is the accounting for shares of those two reserves. Burn the LP, get the current reserves in proportion. Hold the LP, hold a claim on a moving pile, not on the amounts you put in.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to name an LP token as a share of current reserves, not a receipt for the original deposits, and refuse to treat it as a second yield by itself

## Mint and burn

Add token A and token B in the ratio the pool currently wants (close to the reserve ratio, or you get extra impact). The pair mints LP to you. Your share = your LP / total LP. Reserves can then change because of swaps. When you burn, you get share × current reserves, not share × original deposits.

If you deposited 100 A and 100 B, you should not expect 100 and 100 back. You should expect the pile as it now stands, minus fees taken by the protocol if any, plus the fees that stayed in the reserves (the k drift from earlier).

## The LP token is another ERC-20

It has `approve`. Farms will ask for that approve. It can be transferred. It can be faked: a contract that names itself “TOKEN-WBNB LP” without being the pair’s actual LP. Read the LP’s address from the pair (`liquidity token` / the pair itself on Uniswap-v2-style designs, where the pair **is** the LP token). Do not read it from a farm UI first.

On Uniswap-v2-style pairs, the pair contract is both the pool and the LP token. On some later designs, a position is an NFT. Same job, different object. Name which.

## Worked share

Pool reserves 10,000 A and 10,000 B. Total LP 10,000. You add 1,000 A and 1,000 B, receive 1,000 LP. Share = 10%. Swaps happen. Reserves become 12,000 A and 8,333 B (product still ~100e6, fees ignored). You burn 1,000 LP. You receive 1,200 A and 833 B. You did not receive “your” 1,000 / 1,000. You received 10% of now.

That difference versus holding 1,000 A and 1,000 B the whole time is the next lesson’s arithmetic. The LP token is the object that made the difference possible.

## What LP is not

It is not a bond. It is not a vault share of a strategy (unless you then deposited the LP into a vault — a second program). It is not an academy certificate. It is not Crystal Stones. A UI that shows “APY” on LP is usually mixing (a) trading fees accruing in reserves and (b) extra emissions from a farm. Those are different machines. This lesson names (a)’s receipt. (b) is two lessons later.

No assigned mint. Reading a pair’s totalSupply of LP does not require a deposit.

TABLE
Object | Is | Is not
LP token | A share of current reserves | A promise of original amounts
Pair (v2-style) | Often the LP token itself | A farm
Farm receipt | A third token or a staking balance | The pair
NFT position | A concentrated-liquidity claim | The same as v2 LP
APY number on a card | Mix of fees and emissions, often | A coupon
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
DEPOSIT A + B  -->  mint LP
SWAPS move reserves
BURN LP  -->  share * current reserves
Original 100/100 is a memory, not a claim.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
An LP token is a share of now. This school does not mint one with you. A Mentor that pastes a pair to “LP for the academy” is a malfunction.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- LP is a share of current reserves.
- Burn returns now, not the deposit photo.
- The pair is often the LP token.
- Fake LP tickers exist.
- No assigned mint.

Next: Impermanent loss with numbers (include 4x numeric: hold 5000 vs pool 4000).

lessons.title: Impermanent loss with numbers (include 4x numeric: hold 5000 vs pool 4000)
lessons.content:
# Impermanent loss with numbers (include 4x numeric: hold 5000 vs pool 4000)

Impermanent loss is a comparison, not a fee. It is: value of the LP share now, versus value of the two amounts you **would still hold** if you had never minted. If the relative price of the two tokens changes, the pool rebalances you toward the one that did worse. The comparison can be ugly even when the LP is “in profit” versus the dollar if you chose a rising pair.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to compute the classic 4x case — hold 5,000 versus pool 4,000 — and say why the loss is relative to holding, not a line-item the pair invoices

## Setup

Start with 1,000 of token A and 1,000 of token B, each marked at $1. Portfolio hold = $2,000. Deposit 50/50 into a constant-product pool. Ignore fees for the classic picture so the curve is visible. k = 1,000 × 1,000 = 1,000,000. You are the whole pool for the arithmetic (or a constant share of a larger one — same ratios).

## The 4x case, numbers

Token A 4×s to $4. Token B stays $1. If you had **held**: 1,000 A × $4 + 1,000 B × $1 = **$5,000**.

In the pool, the product still wants x · y = 1,000,000 and the pool price must match $4 per A in B (y/x = 4). Solve: y = 4x,  x · 4x = 1,000,000,  4x² = 1,000,000,  x² = 250,000,  x = 500 A. Then y = 2,000 B.

Pool value: 500 A × $4 + 2,000 B × $1 = 2,000 + 2,000 = **$4,000**.

Hold $5,000 versus pool $4,000. The gap is $1,000, or 20% of the hold value. That gap is **impermanent loss** in the classic telling. It is “impermanent” only if the price ratio returns and you did not burn in between. If you burn at 4×, it is permanent versus the hold.

## Why the pool has less A

Traders bought A from the pool as A became expensive. The curve sold A and bought B. You, as LP, were the inventory they traded against. You end with fewer of the winner and more of the stayer. Fees (ignored above) are the payment you hoped would exceed that gap. Sometimes they do. On a violent one-way move with little volume, they do not.

## How to use the number without becoming a desk

The 4× case is a warning label, not a prompt to LP “only stable-stable.” Stable-stable pools have other failures (depeg, hostile token, admin). Volatile pairs have this arithmetic plus those.

This school does not assign a hedge, a “just HODL,” or a farm to out-emit the gap. It assigns: if a poster shows LP value $4,000 after a 4× and does not mention the $5,000 hold, the poster omitted the comparison that defines IL.

Work the same ratios at 2× if you want practice: hold 1,000×2 + 1,000 = 3,000; pool x = 1000/√2 ≈ 707, y ≈ 1,414; value ≈ 1,414 + 1,414 = 2,828. Gap versus 3,000 is smaller than the 4× gap. Bigger relative move, bigger IL. Not a personality. Algebra.

TABLE
State | A units | B units | Value vs $
Start | 1,000 | 1,000 | 2,000
Hold after A 4× | 1,000 | 1,000 | 5,000
Pool after A 4× | 500 | 2,000 | 4,000
IL vs hold | | | 1,000 (20% of hold)
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
HOLD: 1000 A @4 + 1000 B @1 = 5000
POOL:  500 A @4 + 2000 B @1 = 4000
Gap is IL vs hold, not a fee invoice.
Fees (ignored here) are the hoped-for offset.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Hold 5,000 versus pool 4,000 at 4× is the number. This academy does not assign a deposit to “feel” it. Paper is enough.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- IL is versus holding the original amounts.
- At 4×: hold 5,000, pool 4,000.
- The pool sold the winner to traders.
- “Impermanent” dies if you burn here.
- No assigned LP to test IL live.

Next: Farms are emissions plus extra keys.

lessons.title: Farms are emissions plus extra keys
lessons.content:
# Farms are emissions plus extra keys

A farm is usually: stake the LP (or a vault share) in **another** contract, and that contract drips a reward token. The poster adds the drip to the trading-fee APY and prints one large number. You granted a new approve. You accepted a new admin. You took a new token whose job may be to be sold into the same pool you are in.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to split farm APY into pool fees versus emissions, name the extra spender and the extra token, and refuse a combined APY as a single machine

## Two machines

**Pool fees** stay in reserves if the pair works that way. You get them when you burn LP (or as you hold, via k). **Emissions** are a mint or a transfer from a farm contract, often a different ticker. They can be cut, redirected, or worthless. Adding them to fee APY is like adding a salary to a rent yield and calling it “the building.”

If the emission token is the same as one side of the pair, the farm is paying you with inventory that you might be helping to dump. That is not automatically evil. It is a loop you should be able to draw.

## Extra keys

Staking LP requires `approve(farm, LP)`. That is a pull-right on the share of the pile. A hostile or upgraded farm can pull LP and not give it back. Masterchef-style contracts have owner functions: change reward rate, change pool weights, migrate. Timelocks help and are not magic.

A “deposit LP, receive receipt token, receipt token is then staked” is two extra programs. Each has an admin. Each has an ABI.

## Worked split

UI: “120% APY.” Fine print (if any): 18% fees (backward-looking, volume-dependent) + 102% emissions in FARM-TICKER. FARM-TICKER’s daily mint is large versus its pool. The 102% is a unit price times a drip. If FARM-TICKER halves, the poster’s 120% was a screenshot. The 18% was already uncertain.

You still have IL versus hold on the LP. Emissions might cover it. They might not. The UI added them as if they were as sure as the curve.

## Empty yield box

This school does not name a farm. It does not name an emission ticker. It does not tell you to stake LP. Crystal Stones is not a farm reward this academy pays. Academy XP is not an emission. A site that says “stake CST-LP for academy points” is not this course.

If Mentor pastes a masterchef address, that is a malfunction. Revoke lessons still apply to farm spenders you already granted in some other life — this course does not send you hunting.

TABLE
Piece | Source | Can vanish when
Fee APY | Volume in the pair | Volume dies; you already took IL
Emission APY | Farm mint / transfer | Admin, price of reward, end of schedule
LP approve to farm | Your signature | Drain if farm is hostile
Reward token | Another mapping | Tax, mint, thin pool
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
LP  --approve-->  FARM
                    |
                    +-- drips REWARD TOKEN (priced how?)
                    +-- owner can change rates / migrate
UI adds fee APY + emission APY = one poster
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
A farm is emissions plus extra keys. Combined APY is a poster. This academy’s yield box remains empty.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Fees and emissions are different machines.
- A farm wants a pull-right on LP.
- Emission APY is a price times a drip.
- Admins change weights.
- No assigned farm, no CST emissions.

Next: Lockers that do not lock.

lessons.title: Lockers that do not lock
lessons.content:
# Lockers that do not lock

“Lock” on a DeFi poster can mean a time-weighted vote, a UI countdown, a separate contract that still has an admin `withdraw`, or nothing. People hear a vault door. They often get a mapping with a timestamp and a privileged function. Reading the locker is the same job as reading a vault: who can move the pile before your timestamp.

By the end of this lesson you should be able to split vote-escrow, UI timers, and admin-exit lockers, and refuse the word lock as a door until the exit functions are named

## Vote-escrow (ve)

You lock a token (or LP) until a timestamp and receive a non-transferable voting weight that decays. The lock is often real in the sense that **you** cannot call withdraw early. It is not real in the sense that the token’s other functions (tax, mint, upgrade) still run, and in the sense that the locker contract can still have bugs or an escape hatch.

Max lock for max votes is a governance design. It is not a yield. Selling “max lock for 4 years, 80% APR” is a farm poster glued to a governance object.

## UI timers

Some sites show a lock that is only a frontend disable. The contract still allows withdraw. View-source on the website is not view-source on the chain. If `withdraw` has no timestamp check, the lock was a colour on a button.

The inverse: a contract that will not withdraw until T, and a UI that claims you can leave. The UI is then lying in the other direction. Always the ABI.

## Admin exits and “emergency unlock”

A locker with `emergencyWithdraw` for the owner is a locker that does not lock versus the owner. A locker that can `migrate` the underlying to a new contract is a locker that can move your pile. A locker that takes LP and then LP’s pair can still be rug-pulled is a locker of a claim, not of a door.

Worked read: function list shows `lock(amount, weeks)`, `withdraw()`, `emergencyUnlock(address)`, `setPenalty`. Penalty on early exit might apply to you. `emergencyUnlock` might skip your timestamp. Name both.

## What this school will not lock

No assigned ve-lock. No assigned “lock CST for tiers.” Academy ranks are not vote-escrow. Intermediate checkout is not a locker. A chat that says “lock LP 365 days, academy official” is a farm plus a malfunction.

If you already locked something elsewhere, this lesson does not walk it back. It names the object so the next poster cannot use the word lock as a lullaby.

TABLE
Label | Might actually be | Read
ve-lock | Timestamped withdraw disabled for you | Escape hatches; token functions
UI lock | A disabled button | withdraw() with no time check
Admin lock | A pile the owner can migrate | emergency / migrate
Penalty lock | You can leave, minus a fee | Who sets the fee
“Locked liquidity” | A third contract, maybe with unlock | Unlock date and admin
ENDTABLE

DIAGRAM
POSTER: "locked"
    |
    +--> you cannot withdraw until T?  (maybe)
    +--> owner can?                    (read)
    +--> token still mint/tax?         (read)
    +--> UI only?                      (read)
If any answer is shrug, you do not have a door.
ENDDIAGRAM

NOTE
Lock is a word. Exit functions are facts. This academy will not lock your LP, your CST, or your certificate.
ENDNOTE

## Say this out loud

- Lock is not a door until withdraw is read.
- Vote-escrow can be real for you and still have hatches.
- UI timers are not ABIs.
- emergencyUnlock is an owner exit.
- No assigned lock, no CST lock.
